Prevention: Mbili, Meremeta, Mkombozi, Belinde, Kasala, Suma, Kyaka, Pwani, Mkumba, Makutupora, Dodoma
Plant clean cuttings originating from unaffected areas
Use sterilized cutting equipment e.g. sterilize with bleach, fire
Do not move cassava from affected areas. (In areas with brown streak infection, consume cassava locally.)
Monitoring: Monitor for white flies which can spread

Virus: - When leaves first appear (2-3 months after planting), begin observing cassava plants for white fly infestation - Observe flying whiteflies when branches shaken - During scouting, also observe the presence of white flies under cassava leaves - When 5-10 plants per acre are infested, consider taking action

Monitor plants for disease symptoms twice a week for 2-3 months after planting: - Yellow spots on leaves, leaves do not become misshapen like when they are infected by mosaic virus - Stems with dark streaks - Carry out roguing when less than 5% of plants show symptoms
Direct Control: Control white flies using liquid soap mixed with sugar or cooking oil.
Apply soap solution once per week (30 mls liquid soap /litre water or 5-8 g bar soap / litre water)
Seed extract: 50g/liter water with a little soap; Seed powder mix 1:1-1:2 with sawdust/soil; Leaves: 50-150g- 1-2 handful/litre water, soap
Rogue (remove) and burn all infected plants
Restrictions: There are no chemicals against viruses.
If virus symptoms are not yet apparent, you may spray against the virus vector, white fly.
Once the virus is present in the crop, sprays against whiteflies will no longer be effective.
NOT ALLOWED in areas where cassava leaves are harvested for food, because leaf-picking persons may not know that a field has been sprayed.

When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label, such as dosage, timing of application, pre- harvest interval, max number of sprays, restricted re-entry interval, min retreatment interval.
